blocks.text: The reactions in which an electrophile is added to the double bond of an alkene is called electrophilic addition reaction.
Mechanism of electrophilic addition in alkenes

The C=C in alkenes is a region of high electron density making susceptible to attack by electrophiles. Alkenes reacts with an electrophile to give a carbocation intermediate that then reacts with a nucleophile. In the generalized mechanism Figure 11.13, X⁺ represents an electrophile and Y⁻ represents a nucleophile.

blocks.alt: Top: ethene with its double bond shaded and a red curly arrow from the double bond to X+ (electrophile); arrow to X-CH2-CH2+ with a red arrow pointing to the label carbocation. Bottom: the carbocation X-C-C+ with Y- (nucleophile) and a red curly arrow from Y- to C+; arrow to X-CH2-CH2-Y.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.13: Generalized mechanism of electrophilic addition (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.13).

blocks.text: In this chapter, only the mechanism of halogen addition and hydrogen halide addition will be learnt.
1. Halogenation

Halogenation means addition of halogens like chlorine or bromine. When bromine water (a solution of bromine in water having red-brown colour) is added to ethene in an inert solvent like carbon tetrachloride, its reddish brown colour is discharged at once. This reaction is used to identify the unsaturation of an organic compound.
Mechanism
The above reaction proceeds through a three–steps mechanism as given below:

i) Bromine (Br₂) is a non-polar molecule, however, when a bromine molecule gets closer to the double bond of an alkene, the high electron density in the double bond repels the electron pair in Br-Br away from the Br atom. As a result of this, the Br atom closest to the double bond is slightly positive and acts as an electrophile.

blocks.alt: Ethene with its double bond shaded and an outlined arrow labelled High area of electron density, Non-polar molecule. Br2 drawn as two dashed electron clouds: delta+ Br (labelled Electrophile) next to delta- Br: (labelled Induced Dipole), with the note The double bond repels the electrons away from the closest Br atom.
blocks.caption: Step (i): the double bond induces a dipole in Br2 (original drawing after the scheme printed on p260 of the textbook).

blocks.text: ii) The δ⁺ bromine of Br₂ is attacked by the π electrons in the double bond and the partial positive bromine accepts a pair of electrons from the C=C bond in the alkene. This results in the formation of a highly reactive carbocation intermediate.
iii) This carbocation intermediate reacts with the Br⁻ (nucleophile) to make the product. Mechanism is shown below Figure 11.14.

blocks.alt: Mechanism: ethene with a curly arrow from the C=C to the delta+ Br of Br-Br, and a curly arrow from the Br-Br bond to the delta- Br; a red outlined arrow under ethene reads Donates electrons pair to Br+. Arrow marked Room Temp. to the primary carbocation H-CH(Br)-CH(+)-H, attacked by :Br- (curly arrow); a down arrow leads to 1,2-dibromoethane with Br on each carbon.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.14: Electrophilic addition mechanism of ethene and Br2 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.14).

blocks.text: 2. Hydrohalogenation
When an alkene reacts with dry gaseous hydrogen halide at room temperature, the product is a halogenoalkane.

Hydrogen halides are among the simplest examples of polar substances having permanent dipoles that add to alkenes Figure 11.15. All hydrogen halides (HBr,HCl,HI,HF) give this reaction and add across C=C exactly the same way. But, the rate of reaction increases from HF to HI. The actual product formed depends upon whether the alkene is symmetrical or unsymmetrical.

blocks.alt: H-Br with delta+ on H and delta- on Br and a dipole arrow pointing to Br. H is circled in green and labelled Electrophile. Boxed labels: Pulls the electrons more strongly towards itself (Br); Has lower electronegativity than Br so is electron deficient (H).
blocks.caption: Figure 11.15: HBr molecule polarity (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.15).

blocks.text: i) Addition to symmetrical alkenes: When the alkene (e.g. ethene) is symmetrical only one product is theoretically possible. Let us look at the mechanism of addition of HBr to ethene.
Mechanism:

items: Nucleophilic pi-bond attacks the hydrogen in hydrogen halide. Hydrogen bromide gives a bromide ion (Br⁻). Ethene is converted to carbocation by adding hydrogen to one of the double bonded carbons.
The bromide ion (nucleophile) attacks the carbocation to give the addition product Figure 11.16.

blocks.alt: Ethene with a curly arrow from the C=C to the delta+ H of H-Br, and a curly arrow from the H-Br bond to Br. Arrow to the carbocation H-CH2-CH(+)-H attacked by :Br- (curly arrow); a down arrow leads to 1-Bromoethane, alkyl halide, H-CH2-CH(Br)-H.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.16: Electrophilic addition mechanism of HBr to ethene (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.16).

blocks.text: ii) Addition to unsymmetrical alkenes: When the alkene is unsymmetrical, two products are theoretically possible. For example, the addition of HBr to propene can give two products. But experimentally, it has been found that under these conditions, the major product is 2-bromopropane and the minor product is 1-bromopropane.
Markovnikov’s Rule is applicable for addition reactions in alkenes. According to this rule,

blocks.title: Markovnikov’s Rule
blocks.text: “When a polar reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the negative part of the reagent attach to the double bonded carbon which bears the lesser number of hydrogen.”
Mechanism
Propene reacts with HBr in two ways. The mechanism of this reaction involves the following steps.

items: The pi electrons of C=C attacks on partial positive end of H-Br. Hydrogen bromide breaks heterolytically creating bromide ion (electrophile) and hydrogen is added to double bonded carbon with more number of hydrogen, creating a 2º carbocation.
The bromide ion attacks the secondary carbocation to give the major product. The minor product is formed by the attack on primary carbocation Figure 11.17.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The bromide ion (Br⁻) is the nucleophile, not the electrophile: it gives its electron pair to the carbocation, as step ii says.

blocks.alt: Propene drawn with all bonds; a curly arrow from its C=C to the delta+ H of H-Br and one from the H-Br bond to Br. Room Temp: the H adds to the CH2 end giving the secondary carbocation CH3-CH(+)-CH3, attacked by :Br-, giving 2-bromopropane (major product). Room Temp. (lower path): the H adds to the middle carbon giving the primary carbocation CH3-CH2-CH2(+), attacked by :Br-, giving 1-bromopropane (minor product).
blocks.caption: Figure 11.17: Electrophilic addition mechanism of HBr to propene (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.17).

blocks.text: 3. Hydrogenation
Hydrogenation means addition of molecular hydrogen to an alkene in the presence of a catalyst (Ni/ Pt) to form a saturated compound at 250-300 ⁰C.
On industrial scale, this reaction is used to convert vegetable oil into margarine (Banaspati ghee).
4. Hydration
Gaseous alkenes react with steam at high temperature and pressure in the presence of concentrated acid (H₂SO₄) as the catalyst to form alcohols.
Similar to hydrohalogenation, the alkene forms a carbocation intermediate, which is then attacked by OH⁻.
5. Halohydration

Halohydration is a reaction where an alkene reacts with a halogen (such as bromine or chlorine) in the presence of water to form a halohydrin. For ethene (C₂H₄), the reaction specifically produces a bromohydrin or chlorohydrin, depending on the halogen used.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed product CH₃–CH(Br)OH carries Br and OH on the same carbon, and the equation is not balanced. Br and OH add to the two carbons of the double bond: H₂C=CH₂ + Br₂ + H₂O → Br–CH₂–CH₂–OH + HBr. The product is 2-bromoethanol (ethylene bromohydrin), not ‘1-Bromo-2-ethanol’.
6. Epoxidation

blocks.title: Epoxide
blocks.text: The epoxidation of alkenes gives an oxygen-containing three-membered cyclic ether called epoxide.

In the case of ethene (C₂H₄), this reaction can be accomplished using various oxidizing agents. Ethene can also be converted to ethylene oxide using molecular oxygen and metal catalysts. A transition metal catalyst facilitates the reaction, forming an epoxide directly from the alkene. The epoxides can be converted in to diols by acid hydrolysis.

blocks.alt: Ethene + O2, arrow marked Ag, to the epoxide (two CH2 carbons joined to each other and to one O in a three-membered ring), arrow marked H+/H2O, to ethane-1,2-diol, H2C(OH)-CH2(OH).
blocks.caption: Epoxidation of ethene and hydrolysis of the epoxide (original drawing after the scheme printed on p263 of the textbook).

blocks.text: 7. Ozonolysis

Ozonolysis is a method of oxidatively cleaving alkenes using ozone (O₃), a reactive allotrope of oxygen. This reaction is often used to identify the structure of unknown alkenes by breaking them down into smaller, more easily identifiable pieces. Alkenes react with ozone (O₃) to form ozonides, which can be further reduced to carbonyl compounds (aldehydes or ketones), and ultimately to alcohols.

blocks.alt: 1-Propene, H3C-CH=CH2, with O3 gives the ozonide, a five-membered ring of O-O, CH2, O and HC carrying H3C. Zn/H2O gives ethanal (H3C-CHO) + methanal (HCHO), drawn with C=O; reduction gives ethanol, H3C-CH2-OH, and methanol, CH3-OH.
blocks.caption: Ozonolysis of propene (original drawing after the scheme printed on p264 of the textbook).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed scheme shows the formation of the ozonide with a reversible arrow; it is a one-way reaction, drawn above with a single arrow.

blocks.text: 8. Polymerization

blocks.title: Polymerization
blocks.text: Polymerization is the formation of extremely long molecules (polymers) from small reactive molecules that join together (monomers).

Addition polymerization is one of the most important addition reactions of alkenes which form the basis of the plastics industry. Addition polymerization is the reaction in which many monomers containing at least one C=C double bond form long chains of polymers as the only product.

Just like in other addition reactions of alkenes, the π-bond in each C-C bond breaks and then the monomers link together to form new C-C single bonds. A polymer is a long-chain molecule that is made up of many repeating units.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The π-bond that breaks is the one in each C=C double bond of the monomers; a C-C single bond has no π-bond.

blocks.alt: Two rows. n ethene (H2C=CH2), arrow Polymerization, to poly(ethene) drawn as -CH2-CH2- in square brackets with subscript n; labels Monomer and Polymer. n chloroethene (H2C=CHCl), arrow Polymerization, to poly(chloroethene) (PVC), -CH2-CHCl- in square brackets with n.
blocks.caption: Addition polymerisation of ethene and chloroethene (original drawing after the scheme printed on p264 of the textbook).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the printed scheme the PVC repeating unit shows 'C' where chlorine belongs; each second carbon carries Cl, as drawn above.

blocks.title: Interesting Information!
blocks.text: Alkenes, like ethene and propene, are used to create plastics through polymerization. Ethene, for instance, is polymerized to make polyethylene, one of the world’s most common plastics used in bags, bottles, and packaging.
This ball pen is made of PVC
Deducing repeating units

items: A repeating unit is the smallest group of atoms that when connected one after the other make up the polymer chain. It is represented by square brackets in the displayed and general formula.

In poly(alkenes) (such as poly(ethene)) and substituted poly(alkenes) (such as PVC) made of one type of monomer, the repeating unit is the same as the monomer except that the C-C double bond is changed to a C-C single bond.

blocks.alt: n ethene (monomer), arrow, poly(ethene) in square brackets with n (polymer), red arrow, a chain of four CH2 carbons with all H atoms drawn and a brace under two carbons labelled Repeating unit.
blocks.caption: Deducing the repeating unit of poly(ethene) (original drawing after the scheme printed on p265 of the textbook).
